\chapter{Knowing How --- the Verb That Once Meant Taste}
\label{ch:saber}
\hlchaptermodality{389}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I know how to do with sé plus an infinitive, ask someone else with sabes, and tell that apart from what poder says.}

Complete ES-C389-saber: say one thing you know how to do with sé plus an infinitive, ask a partner the same with sabes, and say one thing you know how to do but cannot do today.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[saber]{saber — the verb that started out meaning \textquotedblleft{}to taste\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:ES-C389-saber}



\begin{quote}
Say \emph{I can read}. (\emph{Puedo leer}.) Hold that sentence — it means something narrower than you think.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item poder — \emph{puedo, puedes, puede}.
  \item la sopa and el ajo — how this starts.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sa-BER}, weight on the second beat. The \emph{b} is soft — lips close but never quite meet. The final \emph{r} is one tap. $\to$ pronunciation reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{saber} — \textquotedblleft{}to know.\textquotedblright{} That gloss is the end of the story; the beginning is better.

Latin \textbf{sapere} meant \emph{to taste}, and Spanish still uses it that way daily:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Esta sopa sabe a ajo.} — This soup \textbf{tastes} of garlic.
\end{quote}

Not a second verb that looks the same. It is \emph{saber}, doing its original job.

Tasting to knowing is one short step, and English takes it too: whoever can taste the difference can \emph{tell} the difference. Say \emph{he has taste} and you are not talking about his tongue. So the seam still shows — \emph{sabe a ajo}, it tastes of garlic; \emph{sabe leer}, he knows how to read.

English borrowed pieces of the family from Latin. \textbf{Savour} is \emph{sapor}, \textquotedblleft{}flavour,\textquotedblright{} \emph{sapere}'s own noun. \textbf{Insipid} is \emph{in-} plus \emph{sapidus}, \textquotedblleft{}tasty\textquotedblright{} — what is insipid has no \emph{sapor}. And \emph{sapiens}, the present participle, gave us \emph{\textbf{Homo sapiens}}: read strictly, not the \emph{wise} animal but the \textbf{tasting} one, the animal that tells things apart.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar lens — saber plus an infinitive}]
A plain infinitive straight after \emph{saber} means \textbf{know how to} — a skill you were taught and still have.

\begin{quote}
\emph{Sé leer.} — I know how to read. \emph{¿Sabes escribir?} — Do you know how to write?
\end{quote}

Against the verb you already had:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{} & \textbf{} \\
\midrule
\emph{\textbf{Sé\emph{ leer.\textbf{}}}} & I know how. I learned it. \\
\emph{\textbf{Puedo\emph{ leer.\textbf{}}}} & I am able to right now — there is light. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Both come out as \textquotedblleft{}I can read,\textquotedblright{} and they are not interchangeable. \emph{Sé leer pero hoy no puedo} is ordinary Spanish: the skill is permanent, the opportunity is not.

Two forms to start with. The \emph{yo} form is irregular and very short:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sé} — I know how
  \item \emph{sabes} — you know how
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
You can say what you know how to do, and ask someone else — and you know why the soup and the skill are one verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{sé leer}
  \item \emph{¿sabes escribir?}
  \item \emph{sé leer pero hoy no puedo}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What did \emph{sapere} mean first? (To taste.) Which is the learned skill, \emph{sé leer} or \emph{puedo leer}? (\emph{Sé leer}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
